state.quoted_latest: Aiko Fujita: Aiko: Hana, a kitchen buying from six farms needs someone who knows small suppliers: who pays on time, who delivers when they say. You run a small shop; you know what a late invoice does.

quoted_recent.speaker: Aiko Fujita
quoted_recent.text: Let me tell you who lives there. I visit a pensioner on Orchard Lane, Arthur, eighty-three, whose only hot meal some weeks is the school's, because the meals-on-wheels van was cut. Now Bram's case is real, and I've watched farms go under, so I don't dismiss it. But the motion says make the town buy from local farms, and I've seen what "make" does in a budget meeting when the beet crop fails or a farm's barn burns. Fresh is good, yet a school board cannot promise a fixed price to a mother counting change. Arthur needs the same dinner every Tuesday, not a good dinner three weeks and none the fourth. Steady for farms can mean famine for children when weather turns. I'd rather see it voluntary than made.

quoted_recent.speaker: Bram de Vries
quoted_recent.text: With respect, Aiko, that frozen dinner for Arthur didn't come off a farm, it came off a cutting floor in a budget meeting, and I'll bet my milk cheque the contract went to whoever was cheapest, not whoever was closest. So don't hang a school meal on me, that van wasn't cut by a farmer. And Rin, you're right about the four-month season, so here's what a farmer does when the ground is shut: we store, we freeze, we make cheese, we keep hens laying through December in a warm barn. Nobody said turnips in February. School years run ten months and we fill them all. On volume, a school board can write one contract split across six farms with a root-cellar and a cold room between them. On cost, I'll ask it straight, what does this cost a small business? Nothing, if the town stops paying for trucks. Decided in town, paid for on the farm. That's the line I won't move.

quoted_recent.speaker: Rin Morisaki
quoted_recent.text:
okay bram's doing the thing where he reframes the cut as our fault and then calls it "nothing." first: nobody said the frozen dinner came off a farm, i said the mandate doesn't fix arthur. those are different sentences, bram.

and "nothing, if the town stops paying for trucks" is doing a lot of work. a cold room. a root cellar. a warm barn through december. who built those? who pays the power bill on a january hen barn? the mandate puts the school board on the hook for a fixed price for ten months, but farms can't guarantee that price when diesel spikes or a crop fails, so either the town eats the overrun or we're back to whatever's cheapest come march.

also arthur. nobody in this motion said arthur. kids get first pick, fine, but the second the budget tightens the school meal is the thing that gets renegotiated, and a mandate makes it worse, not better. fight me.

quoted_recent.speaker: Hana Morisaki
quoted_recent.text: Okay, Aiko, you brought Arthur, and I'm glad you did, because he's exactly who I'm thinking about. Those meals-on-wheels cuts weren't farmers' doing, and this motion doesn't take his Tuesday dinner away. If anything, a local contract keeps the school kitchen cooking real food instead of reheating pouches, and that steady kitchen can share the load when the van falters. But Rin, you asked who pays for the cold room, and fair, so let's answer it plainly. Those costs exist whether we buy local or not. A distributor's trucks and warehouses get paid too; we just never see the invoice. Doing it here means the power bill for a January hen barn stays in Sunny Hollow, and Bram's right that we store, freeze, and keep hens laying. I keep the flowers on the table low so people can see each other eat, and I want Arthur at that table, same Tuesday, every Tuesday, probably!!

state.quoted_latest: Victor Hale: Victor: Amara, the night-shift nurse is exempt. Illness, caregiving and shift work are written into every compulsory-voting statute, and emergency-department staff vote by post.

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: Let's figure out what's actually going on here, Victor, because your concession is doing more work than you admit. You say every serious regime exempts illness and caregiving — but that's exactly the point: compulsion only functions if the state can sort genuine abstention from mood, which means paperwork, appeals, and a gatekeeping apparatus we'd never accept in any other civic context. And your forty-percent equalization claim cuts both ways: Australia's turnout gain is real, but informal voting rises alongside it, and the electoral commission has never shown it changes who wins in a way that justifies fining a night-shift nurse. If presence were genuinely equalizing, we'd see it in policy outcomes. We don't. The honest fix is Sofia's pilot — automatic enrolment, weekend voting, postal access. Earn the ballot; don't subpoena it. We oppose.

quoted_recent.speaker: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz
quoted_recent.text: On the equalization claim, I'd want to see the ward-level data before I sign off, because composition effects are not the same as turnout effects. The range I'd defend: compulsory voting plausibly adds five to fifteen points, but the downstream policy shift is modest and contested. The second-order effect nobody on either side is naming is enforcement cost inequality: fines fall hardest on people with unstable addresses, not on the affluent who already vote. Australia's exemptions work, but they work through bureaucracy, and bureaucracy is regressive. On Sofia's pilot, I'll take it seriously, but note the difference between testing a nudge and testing a duty. Automatic enrolment changes the cost of voting; compulsion changes its status. Those are different interventions. What I'd actually want is a staggered rollout in matched wards, measuring turnout, informal votes, and service qual…

quoted_recent.speaker: Sofia Brandt
quoted_recent.text: Daniel, thirty-one percent is a real number and I won't wave it away — but notice what it actually diagnoses: not a missing duty, a missing shortcut. Those parents didn't choose apathy; the polling station was a bus-and-a-buggy haul and the postal deadline fell on half-term. Draw it on a map first: you'd see the problem is three junctions and one form, not the human heart. Mei, I'll take your staggered matched-ward trial gladly — and I'll go further. Run my pilot in two wards and compulsion in two, same matched pair, and measure turnout, informal ballots, and whether the councillor feels a mandate. If duty outperforms convenience, I'll concede. My hypothesis? The fine buys you presence, never voice. Daniel, your Year 9 parents' evening gets its turnout through coffee and a car park; do that. We oppose.

quoted_recent.speaker: Daniel Osei
quoted_recent.text: Sofia says coffee and a car park, and honestly, she's half right — I've stood in that hall handing out tea. But here's what she's missing. The parents who don't come don't come because nobody compels them, and that's fine for a parents' evening — we follow up by phone, we cope. Voting is different. When thirty-one percent choose the council, the other sixty-nine percent still live under it. Now, Mei wants a staggered trial, and I'd support that. But Sofia calls a trial of convenience versus a duty, and the pair aren't symmetrical: convenience lowers the cost, duty raises the stake. They can run together. My own school does both — we ring parents and we require attendance. Nobody calls the register coercive. So yes, test it in matched wards. My prediction: turnout rises in both, but the mandate question — does the councillor feel answerable to the whole ward — only moves wher…

state.quoted_latest: Victor Hale: Victor: The medicine is overstated. No clinical study shows homework causes sleep disorders; adolescent sleep loss is screens and caffeine, as any physician will tell you.

quoted_recent.speaker: Daniel Osei
quoted_recent.text: Thank you, Kai. I'll start where I always start: Monday morning. Last term I stood in our staffroom and watched a Year 9 boy, Callum, fall asleep at his desk before registration. He'd been up until midnight finishing three subjects' worth of worksheets. His mum works nights. Who does that homework, I asked the teachers — Callum, or his exhausted family? The evidence is blunt: homework barely helps primary pupils and shows only modest gains in secondary, while it widens the gap between kids with quiet bedrooms and kids without. Tonight I'm not asking you to ban learning. I'm asking: what would we teach differently if the school day were the honest unit of work? Let's find out.

quoted_recent.speaker: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz
quoted_recent.text: It depends, and here's on what: the design of the abolition and what replaces it. I'll grant you homework is unevenly distributed and often poorly designed — the evidence on that is real. But the leap from "badly designed homework exists" to "abolish it" is where Daniel and Amara will need to do work, because the second-order effect is consolidation: time reallocated to households that can buy tutoring, and displaced to the same students already ahead. Anyone who gives you one number on learning outcomes is selling something; the literature gives ranges, and the ranges shift by age, subject and dose. Worth noting, too, that ambitious working-time pilots skew heavily toward sectors where work is self-paced — seventy-one percent professional services, only nine round-the-clock [1]. Schools are not that. So the burden on the motion is to show the replacement actually reaches the stud…

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: Thanks, Kai. Let's figure out what's actually going on with homework, because the honest answer is we've inherited it, not tested it. The evidence base is weak and inconsistent, yet the load keeps growing — and the burden falls hardest on kids with fewer resources at home. My question for the room: what problem is homework actually solving that class time can't? If we can't answer that, we're mandating something on faith. What does hold up: sleep loss, family stress, and widening gaps. I'm not against practice — I'm against unproven volume. Abolish the default, keep what we can defend with evidence.

quoted_recent.speaker: Victor Hale
quoted_recent.text: Kai, before I concede anything, I define my terms, because Daniel has just handed us a gift and I intend to unwrap it carefully. Three points. First, note the "speed, not direction" turn [1]: Daniel no longer defends homework's value; he indicts its excess. Once both sides accept the goal — rest, fairness, family time — this debate is about implementation, not abolition, and the side with a timetable wins it. state.quoted_latest: Rin Morisaki: Rin: and the animals, sure, but livestock get used to noise. it's one night a year, and farms by the airfield have cows grazing under jets.

quoted_recent.speaker: Aiko Fujita
quoted_recent.text: Let me tell you who lives there. Last November I cycled out to the Kellerman house on Mill Road, where Mrs. Kellerman, eighty-three, keeps her oxygen tank beside the kitchen chair. Her neighbor's boy sets off fireworks in the alley every festival, and each year her daughter calls me because the smoke and the bangs terrify her mother into a night of breathlessness. I am not against joy. I am against the assumption that joy belongs only to those who can tolerate the noise. There are infants on that street, there are veterans, there are dogs who will not stop shaking until morning. Health isn't a statistic when you've held the hand. A silent festival is not a lesser festival. It is simply one everyone can attend.

quoted_recent.speaker: Hana Morisaki
quoted_recent.text: Kai! You came to watch—maybe. Alright, opening statement for the opposition, with Rin at my side like a good little sister who definitely didn't try to bribe me with mochi. Here it is: fireworks are the heartbeat of the Sunny Hollow festival, a shared pulse of oohs and aahs that bonds neighbors like petals in one bouquet. My flower shop sits near the station, and every year I watch kids press their noses to the glass, counting down. Ban that spark and you dim a memory-maker. Noise and safety matter, of course, but a ban is a sledgehammer where we need pruning shears—shorter shows, quieter shells, set zones, cleaning crews. We can bloom responsibly without uprooting joy. Probably. Rin, back me up before Aiko feasts on me.

quoted_recent.speaker: Bram de Vries
quoted_recent.text: Decided in town, paid for on the farm — that's this whole fireworks business in one line, Kai. Every year the town council votes itself a party and my cows pay the bill. I've got sixty head, and come festival night I've got sixty panicked animals running fences because somebody wanted pretty colours in the sky. Last year I lost a calf to a broken leg from it. You tell me what that costs a small farm. My neighbour's dog won't eat for two days after. So the motion's simple: if the town wants a celebration, celebrate without terrorising every creature in earshot. People who've actually done the work know you don't spook stock for a bit of noise. That's my piece.

state.quoted_latest: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz: Mei: There's a legal duty here. The city must provide emergency care within a set time; spend the surplus elsewhere and a judicial review could undo it.

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: Let's figure out what's actually going on before we spend the money. A hospital is where you go when something has already gone badly wrong; a clinic is where you go so it doesn't. If this house spends the surplus on one gleaming building downtown, we buy inpatient beds and a ribbon-cutting, but we don't buy earlier blood-pressure checks, earlier diabetes care, earlier mental-health visits, and all the costly emergency admissions those prevent. I'd want to ask the proposers two things: what's your current wait time for a routine appointment, and what share of your ER visits are conditions a clinic could have managed? If those numbers are ugly, the surplus is better spent on clinics. That said, I'll flag one caveat: if your ICU or trauma capacity is genuinely collapsing, that changes the evidence. What does your data actually show?

quoted_recent.speaker: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz
quoted_recent.text: It depends, and here's on what. The motion frames this as hospital versus clinics, but the real question is marginal returns at the system level, and the honest answer is a range, not a number. Capital-heavy hospitals buy you acute capacity and high fixed costs; distributed clinics buy you throughput, earlier intervention, and cheaper marginal visits, but only if you can staff them, which is the binding constraint nobody puts on the poster. The plausible effect sizes I'd entertain are modest and genuinely uncertain, so I'd want to know the catchment's case-mix, its avoidable-admissions rate, and its vacancy data before committing. And note the second-order effect: a shiny new hospital can cannibalise the workforce that would otherwise make clinics function, so you may buy beds and lose primary care. Anyone who gives you one number is selling something.

quoted_recent.speaker: Victor Hale
quoted_recent.text: Three points, and a preamble, because a debate is won at the definitional threshold. First: define "surplus." A one-time windfall is not a recurring revenue stream, and a hospital is a capital commitment with decades of operating costs behind it. Second: define "rather than." If the proposition means exclusively, it forbids the cheaper, faster, more distributable option — clinics — in favor of the most expensive, slowest, most concentrated one. Third: define "spend." Money placed into concrete is money removed from flexibility. My friends will speak of beds and healing; I ask only that we count. Cui bono — who benefits? The district with the ribbon-cutting, not necessarily the patient. I reserve the remainder of my time.

quoted_recent.speaker: Sofia Brandt
quoted_recent.text: Draw it on a map first, Kai — a hospital is a point on a map, clinics are a network of points, and those are different geometries. A hospital catches everyone who arrives, but only once they're already sick; a clinic network catches people where they live, before the trip becomes an emergency. My instinct is you don't get that network back once you've spent the surplus on one destination build. Show me the ambulance travel times across the wards and the routine-appointment waits and I'll tell you which one the city actually needs. But if the acute capacity is genuinely failing, say so — I'll change my mind on the data, not on the slogan.

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: I'll take Mei's constraint seriously: staffing is binding, and Victor's right that a windfall isn't a revenue stream. That actually strengthens my case, not weakens it. A hospital's decades of operating costs are people; if you can't staff beds, you've built a monument. Sofia, I'll move on one condition — if the ambulance travel times show whole wards beyond any safe acute window, that's a genuine access failure and I'd change my emphasis. But absent that, the evidence still favors distributed clinics, because they buy earlier intervention and cheaper marginal visits. So my question back to the house: define "rather than" as exclusive, and show me the vacancy data. Otherwise we're financing concrete and calling it care.

quoted_recent.text: Three points on the rebuttal. quoted_recent.speaker: Daniel Osei
quoted_recent.text: Thank you, Kai. I'll keep this simple, because I've got a school to get back to. I'm Daniel Osei, headteacher of a large comprehensive, and I want to tell you about my Year 9s. Last term I stood at the gate at half seven and watched kids eat cereal out of a bag, walking. Their first lesson began at 8:40 and half of them weren't awake for it. The evidence on adolescent body clocks is real; I've watched it walk through my doors for eleven years. A later start isn't indulgence, it's timing. But I'll say the difficult part plainly: whoever votes for this must also answer my caretaker, my bus drivers, my parents on shifts. Who does the work on Monday morning? If you can't answer that, the motion stays theory. I can answer it. Let's talk.

quoted_recent.speaker: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz
quoted_recent.text: It depends, and here's on what: a ten o'clock start shifts costs rather than removing them. Before celebrating the chronobiology, note who absorbs the change: transport networks on peak-hour pricing, parents on rigid shifts, and schools already running staggered rotas. My lab looked at compressed-hours evidence and only 71% of the pilot organisations were in professional services, software, marketing or the non-profit sector, with just nine covering round-the-clock services [1]. That is a weak base for a universal reform. The plausible effects run from modest attendance gains of, say, 2–5% in affluent catchments to neutral or negative in low-income areas where after-school care collapses. The second-order effect: an even later finish pushes extracurriculars, paid work and homework into the evening. Anyone offering one number is selling something.

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: Thank you, Kai. Let's figure out what's actually going on with adolescent sleep, because the evidence here is unusually clear. During puberty, the circadian clock shifts later by roughly two hours, so a teenager told to sleep at ten simply cannot fall asleep at ten. The result is a chronic sleep debt: the average secondary pupil gets under seven hours against a nine-hour need. That debt shows up as poorer attention, worse mood, and higher rates of anxiety and depression. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the CDC both recommend start times no earlier than 8:30. So the honest question isn't whether ten is convenient for adults, it's whether we're currently asking children to learn while sleep-deprived. I'd argue that's a public-health problem we can fix with a timetable. I'll hand to Daniel.

state.quoted_motion: This house would start the secondary-school day at ten

quoted_recent.speaker: Bram de Vries
quoted_recent.text: Hana talks about flowers, I'll talk about cows. You don't open the pasture gate and hope the herd finds water — you check where they'll drink first. Same with a high street. Close it to cars on a Saturday and where does my milk truck park? Where do the older customers who drive in from the outlying farms leave their cars? Decided in town, paid for on the farm. Every weekend closure means fewer paying customers through my market stall, and I've counted them — a third come by car. You say you gain the whole street. Maybe. quoted_recent.speaker: Hana Morisaki
quoted_recent.text: Bram, I love you dearly, but you just proved our point!! You said a third of your customers come by car—so two-thirds don't, and on Saturdays that two-thirds is squeezed onto narrow pavements while the cars get the whole road! Dad, side streets won't choke like you fear; every town that's tried this—York, Ghent, Pontevedra—found traffic didn't just shift, it disappeared, because people stopped making pointless trips. And your milk truck? Deliveries before ten, permits, done. Aiko's Mrs. Okada is the whole argument in one person. We're not gutting the fish, we're finally letting the street breathe. Probably!

quoted_recent.speaker: Takeshi Morisaki
quoted_recent.text: Now, Hana, you're quoting York and Ghent like they're stops on my old line, but those towns planned this for years—permits, loading bays, bus routes. You've got a motion, not a timetable. And two-thirds walking doesn't mean two-thirds buying; it means foot traffic, not till traffic. Bram's the one with receipts. Aiko's Mrs. Okada deserves a safe pavement, and I'll fight for that, but you don't fix one crossing by closing the whole line. You widen the pavement, you lower the speed limit, you put in lights that actually give walkers a head start. Slow the trains, don't derail them. Closing a street to solve a traffic problem is like cutting the brake line to fix a squeak—too much, too fast. Right on schedule.

quoted_recent.speaker: Aiko Fujita
quoted_recent.text: Let me tell you who lives there. Kenji, on Mill Lane, ninety-one, uses a walker and a mobility scooter his son drives over twice a week to charge and load. I am not against permits and loading bays; I am saying design them before the closure, not after. Bram's stall and Kenji's son are both real. So widen the pavement, yes, but at weekends give the road to the many who walk it and the few who cannot drive. Deliveries by ten, a taxi rank on both ends, blue-badge bays kept clear and close, and a shuttle for the outlying farms. That is a plan, not a hope.

quoted_recent.speaker: Bram de Vries
quoted_recent.text: Aiko's the only one on that side who's done the arithmetic, I'll give her that. Kenji's son, my stall, the elderly from the outlying farms — she's named them. As written, it's a gate swung shut and a shrug about who feeds the cows. Decided in town, paid for on the farm.

quoted_recent.text: Let me tell you who lives there. Fresh is good, yet a school board cannot promise a fixed price to a mother counting change. Arthur needs the same dinner every Tuesday, not a good dinner three weeks and none the fourth. Steady for farms can mean famine for children when weather turns. I'd rather see it voluntary than made.

quoted_recent.speaker: Amara Okafor
quoted_recent.text: Thanks, Kai. Let's figure out what's actually going on here, because the evidence matters more than the slogan. Sugary drinks are the single largest source of added sugar in most diets, and they're uniquely easy to over-consume because liquid calories don't trigger fullness the way food does. The strongest real-world data comes from Mexico, Berkeley, and Chile: taxes of ten to twenty percent reduce purchases, with the biggest drops among lower-income households, who also face the highest rates of type 2 diabetes. One thing I'd ask the other side upfront: if not price, what mechanism scales fast enough to reach millions of people? I'm not claiming this fixes everything. It's one lever, and I'll flag honest uncertainty about long-term health outcomes. But the direction of evidence is clear enough to act.

quoted_recent.speaker: Victor Hale
quoted_recent.text: Three points, and I begin with a definition, because the motion hides behind a word. "Sugary" — defined by whom, and at what threshold? A gram? A gram per liter? Already the tax's architects disagree among themselves. Second: this is a regressive instrument. It extracts money from the poorest households in proportion to their means while the wealthy barely notice. Regressive taxation dressed as public health is still regressive taxation — a wolf in wool, and we should say so plainly. Third: the stated goal, health, does not follow from the mechanism, taxation. If you want health outcomes, legislate health outcomes; if you want revenue, admit you want revenue. Define your terms, Councilor. Until you do, this motion asks us to tax a word we cannot even measure. The opposition rests.

quoted_recent.speaker: Mei Tanaka-Ruiz
quoted_recent.text: It depends, and here's on what. The evidence on sugary-drink taxes is better than Victor and Daniel will admit, but let me give you a range rather than a slogan. On health outcomes, the chain from purchase to BMI to disease is long and the evidence gets thinner at each link, so anyone quoting a single mortality figure is selling something. The second-order effect that matters most: the tax is regressive on paper but progressive in health incidence, because sugary-drink consumption concentrates among lower-income households who bear the largest avoidable disease burden. Design matters, earmarking matters, and my colleague Amara will take the design question from here.

quoted_recent.text: Oh, Aiko's going for the heart straightaway, and honestly, I get it. But Kai and I have been over this a dozen times, so here we go. Our position is simple: banning video games for under-twelves on school nights punishes the many for the choices of a few, and it hands parents a rule instead of a relationship. That boy on the hill doesn't need a console locked away; he needs someone to close the gap at home, and a blanket ban won't do that, it'll just make gaming the forbidden fruit and push it into sneaky hours. Games are where kids learn to fail safely, collaborate, and unwind, the same way my family unwinds over dinner. And like Grandma wrote, even leftovers become tomorrow's onigiri if you handle them gently [2]. Give families tools, not prohibitions. Probably.

quoted_recent.speaker: Bram de Vries
quoted_recent.text: I'll grant you the boy, Aiko. I've got a farmhand whose lad is the same story, and I've seen what a tired ten-year-old looks like at six in the morning. But let me talk plain about this motion, because I think it's the wrong tool aimed at the wrong ditch. You don't fix a broken fence by banning the whole field. A console in a house with a parent coming home at three is a symptom, not the cause. My neighbour's girl, same age, plays an hour after her chores and does fine. Now you tell me what it costs a small family to enforce a rule a government decided in town. It's the parents who pay it, in arguments and guilt, while the real problem goes unaddressed. So I'm with the proposition on the principle that school nights need protecting, but I want to hear why a blanket ban and not a bedtime the household actually keeps.

quoted_recent.speaker: Aiko Fujita
quoted_recent.text: Let me tell you who lives there. Mrs. Okada, eighty-one, whose grandson visits on Tuesdays with a handheld and a bad grade, and she tells me the machine is the only thing that stays quiet with him. I hear you, Rin — but a handrail isn't forbidden fruit. It's the same as the seatbelt I buckle without a tantrum. And Bram, you're right the fence is broken. So we fix two fences: one at home, one in law. Because the parents who most need the bedtime are the ones too exhausted to hold it, and a rule that stands behind them is lighter, not heavier, than a guilt they carry alone. Age twelve is imperfect, yes. So is every speed limit. We don't abolish them because some drivers are careful. Health isn't a statistic when you've held the hand of a child who couldn't stay awake in class.
